items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that we can use the second derivative to determine the concavity of a differentiable function [MATH: f(x)\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: f(x)] is concave up on an interval [MATH: (a,b)] if [MATH: f''(x) > 0] on [MATH: (a,b),] while
- [MATH: f(x)] is concave down on an interval [MATH: (a,b)] if [MATH: f''(x) < 0] on [MATH: (a,b).]

Content:
So, to determine intervals of concavity of [MATH: f(x)] by looking at the graph of [MATH: f'(x),] we need to pay attention to where [MATH: f'(x)] is increasing or decreasing.

Content:
- If [MATH: f'(x)] is increasing, then [MATH: f''(x)>0,] which means [MATH: f(x)] is concave up.

[IMG: /graphics/33e6fb629b9ad571f799ea5555ddf530]

Content:
- If [MATH: f'(x)] is decreasing, then [MATH: f''(x)<0,] which means [MATH: f(x)] is concave down.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fc6e4154d6f2a5a1b727733c9d45f9c8]

Content:
Also, recall that [MATH: f(x)] has an inflection point at [MATH: x=a] if [MATH: f''(x)] changes its sign around [MATH: x=a.] So, to determine the inflection points of [MATH: f(x)] by looking at a graph of [MATH: f'(x),] we need to pay attention to where [MATH: f'(x)] switches from increasing to decreasing (or vice versa).

Content:
In other words, we need to pay attention to relative extrema on the graph of [MATH: f'(x).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c70ec99c8694dc7edeaa2320f7fc4afa]

  • When [MATH: f'(x)] is decreasing, we have [MATH: f''(x)< 0.]

The function [MATH: f(x)] has an inflection point at [MATH: x=a,] if the following two conditions are satisfied:

  • [MATH: f''(x)=0] or [MATH: f''(x)] is undefined, and

  • [MATH: f''(x)] changes its sign (from negative to positive or vice versa) at that point.

We summarize the information from the given graph in the table below:

Note that the sign of [MATH: f''(x)] does not change at [MATH: x=-1,] and so this is not a point of inflection.

sections.normalized_html:
The graph [MATH: y=g'(x),] the derivative of [MATH: y=g(x),] is shown below. Which of the following statements must be true?

  1. [MATH: g(x)] has a relative maximum at [MATH: x=1.5]

  2. [MATH: g(x)] has a relative minimum at [MATH: x=5]

  3. [MATH: g(x)] has an inflection point at [MATH: x=3.5]
sections.readable_text:
The graph [MATH: y=g'(x),] the derivative of [MATH: y=g(x),] is shown below. Which of the following statements must be true?

1. [MATH: g(x)] has a relative maximum at [MATH: x=1.5]
2. [MATH: g(x)] has a relative minimum at [MATH: x=5]
3. [MATH: g(x)] has an inflection point at [MATH: x=3.5]

[IMG: /graphics/1fafcaaeca9a1fdebf8917e156c4f395]

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that [MATH: y=g'(x)] intersects the [MATH: x]-axis at the points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] as shown below.

An extremum of [MATH: y=g(x)] occurs when the graph [MATH: y=g'(x)] changes its sign. Checking the first derivative at the points [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] we see that

  • the point [MATH: A,] at [MATH: x=1.5,] is a relative maximum of [MATH: g(x)] since the derivative [MATH: g'(x)] switches from positive to negative, and

  • the point [MATH: B,] at [MATH: x=5,] is a relative minimum of [MATH: g(x)] since the derivative [MATH: g'(x)] switches from negative to positive.

Therefore, statements I and II are true.

Now, an inflection point may occur where the second derivative [MATH: y=g''(x)] is zero (the tangent line to [MATH: y=g'(x)] is horizontal) or [MATH: y=g''(x)] does not exist (a rapid change in the slope). Indeed, at the point [MATH: x=3.5,] which we label as [MATH: C,] we see that the slope of [MATH: g'(x)] is zero, meaning that [MATH: g''(x)=0.]

We obtain an inflection point if the slope of the tangent line to [MATH: y=g'(x)] changes its sign. Thus, we have an inflection point at [MATH: C], where the slope goes from negative to positive. Therefore, statement III is true.

In conclusion, all three statements are true.
